DRAFT TRAFFIC CALMING GUIDELINES  CITY OF ALHAMBRA
 Executive Summary
  A traffic request is an easy and straightforward way for citizens to
communicate their concerns regarding traffic safety. The City reviews
each citizen's request to ensure that the proposed location and
circumstances meet all the criteria outlined in this document and are
allowed by City Standards, City Municipal Code, California Manual on
Uniform Traffic Control Devices (CA MUTCD), and State law. To ensure
that resources are used efficiently, requests submitted to the City will
follow specific steps, starting with an initial review and, if applicable,
followed by considerations of traffic calming measures in Levels 1, 2, and
3.

  An initial review will investigate the location's existing r o a d w a y
c o n d i t i o n s and collision history. If the results of this review indicate
that the street and/or intersection warrants additional traffic investigation,
the City will conduct further study, which could include a collection of
traffic counts, speed surveys, and pedestrian counts as appropriate to
thoroughly comprehend the issues at the location. Based on the data
collected and following the proper guidelines, engineering staff will
evaluate and recommend suitable traffic calming measures.

  Traffic calming measures work best when incorporated into a
programmatic approach that includes a planning process, overall
community participation, and public safety service input. The main
objective of this approach is to encourage citizens to become actively
involved throughout the process. In this way, the City and the community
can work together to create long-term solutions.

  3|Page
DRAFT TRAFFIC CALMING GUIDELINES  CITY OF ALHAMBRA
 Traffic Calming Request Process:

Step 1: Resident(s) may notify the City of traffic concerns on their streets
by submitting a Citizen Request Application Form, available on the City’s
website or from City Hall. The request may also be submitted to the City
via a phone app being developed by the City.

To demonstrate neighborhood support, the City asks residents to please
provide signatures from five (5) additional residents living in the requested
area. One (1) signature per address. This preliminary concurrence by
adjacent neighbors ensures that there is likely community support for the
request before the city invests considerable time, effort, and budget
investigating the request.

Step 2: Upon receipt of the application, City staff will acknowledge the
request and initiate a preliminary review. This review will include
evaluating existing conditions, reviewing a 3-year collision history using
the Statewide Integrated Traffic Records System (SWITRS) to gain a better
understanding of any particular safety issue, and determining the street’s
eligibility for further study. This could include determining if the street is
considered a “local/collector” or “residential” roadway as defined in the
California Vehicle Code (CVC) (Section 515), and/or is in a school zone.
City Staff will determine each street's functional classification based on the
Caltrans California Road System – Functional Classification map.

Public Works will inform the resident(s) of the next steps in the traffic
review process. If applicable, the Alhambra Police Division will be
consulted to assess whether installing a speed trailer and additional
enforcement would be beneficial.

Step 3: Following the implementation of Level 1 measures as described
next, the City will determine if the location is eligible for Level 2 traffic
measures. A street that has already implemented Level 1 measures will be
automatically considered under Level 2 and/or Level 3 criteria. This phase
includes additional data collection, such as speed and volume

  4|Page
DRAFT TRAFFIC CALMING GUIDELINES  CITY OF ALHAMBRA
 measurements, pedestrian counts, and field observations, as appropriate.

Traffic Calming Approval Process
The City’s Traffic Engineering Division will develop recommendations to
address motorized traffic, bicycle traffic, and pedestrian mobility concerns
along a corridor or intersection. Upon completion of the engineering
study, these recommendations will be presented to the Alhambra
Transportation Commission for review. Once approved by the Alhambra
Transportation Commission, the item will then be taken to the City Council
for final approval of the recommendations. After City Council’s final
approval, the item will then be placed onto a priority list based upon
available funding. Approved Transportation Commission items will be
brought to the City Council on a quarterly basis for review and potential
budget allocation.

Higher cost items such as signal modifications, flashing beacon
installations, and lighting enhancements— may require the City to pursue
grant funding. All traffic improvement projects will be added to a master
list and prioritized based on merit, community input, and safety needs.
This will ensure that any financial commitments are made transparently,
aligned with available funding sources, and integrated into the City's
larger mobility goals.

Reconsideration of Traffic Calming Requests

Traffic calming measures which have been studied under these guidelines
and have been shown not to meet the minimum thresholds for installation,
will be evaluated no sooner than two (2) years after the first evaluation,
unless an earlier review is deemed necessary by the City’s Public Works
Department due to significant changes in traffic patterns or safety concerns.

  5|Page
DRAFT TRAFFIC CALMING GUIDELINES  CITY OF ALHAMBRA
 Evaluation of Traffic Calming Measures
Implemented

To ensure a systematic and data-driven approach to traffic calming, traffic
measures should be in place for a minimum evaluation period before
determining their effectiveness and considering progression to higher
levels.

  • It is recommended that Level 1 measures be in place or applied for
  at least three to six months, allowing sufficient time for driver
  behavior adjustments and data collection. During this period,
  periodic assessments, including speed studies, traffic volume counts,
  and field observations, should be conducted to gauge the impact of
  enforcement and educational efforts.

  • If the evaluation demonstrates that traffic concerns persist despite
  Level 1 applications, the location will be considered for further
  analysis and potential escalation to Level 2 measures.

  • It is recommended that Level 2 measures be in place for a minimum
  of 12 months to measure their effectiveness before any street is
  elevated to Level 3 and being studied for the applicable eligibility
  criteria.

This structured approach ensures that all available low-cost and non-
physical strategies are fully utilized before advancing to more intensive
traffic-calming solutions.

Revisions to the Traffic Calming Guidelines
The Public Works Department is authorized, with the City Manager's
concurrence, to modify these guidelines as needed with respect to costs
to stay current with the state of the practice and Federal and State
regulations. However, significant modifications to the policy guidelines will
be brought to the City Council for review and approval.

  6|Page
DRAFT TRAFFIC CALMING GUIDELINES  CITY OF ALHAMBRA
 Role of the Transportation Commission

The Transportation Commission is an advisory body to the City Council.
Traffic Calming Measures evaluated by city staff will be presented to the
Transportation Commission for their concurrence and as a step to receiving
public input about Traffic Calming Measures requested by the residents.
Should the Transportation Commission concur with staff recommendations
to install a device, their recommendation will be forwarded to the City
Council for consideration and approval.

Should the Transportation Commission concur with the staff
recommendation that a particular device or measure is not warranted at the
time, the results of the staff’s findings and the Commission’s consideration
will be communicated to the resident(s) requesting a traffic measure.

Residents will be notified of when their item is going before the
Transportation Commission and will have the opportunity to address the
commissioners on their item.

Finally, should the Transportation Commission disagree with staff’s
recommendations, the staff report to the City Council will document both
staff and Transportation Commission recommendations.

Appeal Process

Each requested item will go before the City Transportation Commission
and the City Council. Residents will be notified in advance of these
meetings and can attend in person. At both meetings, residents will be
given the opportunity to speak before the Commissioners/Council
Members on their item. Once the City Council gives final approval, the
decision will be final, and no further appeals can be made.

  7|Page
DRAFT TRAFFIC CALMING GUIDELINES  CITY OF ALHAMBRA
 Level 1 | Initial Review Non-Physical Traffic Calming
M easures – Public Education, Enforcement, and
Speed Display Trailer
Level 1 measures include, but are not limited to, non-physical or minor changes
to the roadway environment. Requests regarding traffic speeding or traffic
volume concerns will be considered for residential streets with the street
designation of local or collector roadways for implementation of Level 1
measures before consideration of Level 2 measures. Please refer to the Traffic
Calming Request Process steps 1-3. Typical measures for Level 1 are:

  1. Traffic Education Campaign:

  This may include flyers, neighborhood meetings, school meetings, and other
  notices to engage the community. It will focus on raising awareness of what
  might be considered excessive traffic volumes or cut-through traffic, the pros
  and cons of painting crosswalks, appropriate use of traffic control devices such
  as stop signs, school signing and marking issues, the use of warning signs and
  speed differentials, emphasizing the gap between vehicle speeds and posted
  speed limits. Brochures for Traffic Measures can be found on the City’s website
  or in person at City Hall. See Figure 1 for an example of the campaign materials
  that could be used in this initiative.

  a. Pros
  i. It can be effective and inexpensive.
  ii. Involves and empowers citizens.
  iii. Works well with other mitigation tools.
  b. Cons
  i. It may be difficult to measure effectiveness.
  ii. It can be time-consuming.
  iii. It may take time to be effective.
  iv. Effectiveness may decrease over time.
  c. Components: Distribution of educational materials,
  community meetings, and public notices.
  d. Cost: Low

  8|Page
DRAFT TRAFFIC CALMING GUIDELINES  CITY OF ALHAMBRA
   Figure 1: Example of traffic education materials, including flyers and notices in neighborhood
  and school campaigns.

  9|Page
DRAFT TRAFFIC CALMING GUIDELINES  CITY OF ALHAMBRA
   2. Targeted Police Enforcement:

  Enforcement of speeds, turning movements, and other moving or parking
  violations. See Figure 2 for an example of police enforcement, where officers
  monitor traffic at key locations.

  a. Pros
  i. Great in achieving temporary results.
  ii. Serves to inform the public that speeding and other
  traffic law violations are undesirable behaviors for
  which there are consequences.
  b. Cons
  i. The effect is not permanent.
  c. Components:  Focused  enforcement of traffic
  regulations, including speed limits and parking
  violations.
  d. Cost: Depends on Police Budget/Resources

  Figure 2: Example of targeted police
  enforcement, showing officers monitoring
  traffic at key location

  10 | P a g e
DRAFT TRAFFIC CALMING GUIDELINES  CITY OF ALHAMBRA
   3. Temporary Placement of Speed Display Radar Trailer:

  Speed Radar Trailers may be placed at one or more locations along the
  street or in the neighborhoods. See Figure 3 for an illustration of a
  typical speed radar trailer set up in a neighborhood.

  a. Pros
  i. Good education tool.
  ii. Very good public relations tool.
  iii. Useful especially in school and construction zones
  where spot speed reduction is important.
  iv. Educates drivers on traffic and speeding issues in the area.
  v. The unit is portable and can be moved from street to street.
  b. Cons
  i. Requires periodic enforcement to be effective.
  ii. Effective for a limited duration.
  iii. Requires personnel to move units from one street to
  another.
  c. Components: Mobile radar trailers will be deployed to
  display vehicle speeds as compared to the posted speed
  limit.
  d. Cost: Low

  11 | P a g e
DRAFT TRAFFIC CALMING GUIDELINES  CITY OF ALHAMBRA
   Figure 3: Example of a speed display radar trailer in use,
  placed temporarily on a residential street to raise
  awareness of speeding.

  12 | P a g e
DRAFT TRAFFIC CALMING GUIDELINES  CITY OF ALHAMBRA
 Level 2 | Low - Moderate Cost: Physical Traffic
Measures
Traffic Calming measures in Level 2 are a group of low to moderate level
enhancements that apply minor physical changes to the roadway
environment. Recommendations in Level 2 may include signage,
pavement markings and legends, parking edge lines, turning movement
restrictions, curve and advance warning signs, commercial vehicle
restrictions and solar speed feedback signs. Level 2 measures will be
considered only after Level 1 measures have been implemented and if
the location meets the Qualifying Criteria for Level 2 review. The focus is
on community-supported measures that are relatively easy to implement
and are cost-effective solutions.

Qualifying Criteria for Level 2:

The City will evaluate requests for implementing Level 2
n e i g h b o r h o o d traffic calming measures on local or collector streets
based on the following criteria:

  1. Street Classification: Under Caltrans California Road System Street
  Classification maps, the street must be classified as a local street or
  collector street (not an arterial) and primarily residential in land use.
  2. Residential Frontage: The street must have residential frontage
  that aligns with the California Vehicle Code (CVC) criteria for local
  street designation and speed limit determination. This requires a
  density of:
  a. At least 13 separate dwelling units or business structures per
  ¼ mile on one side of the street, or;
  b. At least 16 dwelling units or business structures per ¼
  mile on both sides.
  3. Traffic Volume: The street should have at least 500 vehicles
  traveling in both directions daily.

  13 | P a g e
DRAFT TRAFFIC CALMING GUIDELINES  CITY OF ALHAMBRA
   4. Speed Criteria: Speed studies documenting the 85th percentile
  speed in a 24-hour period will be reviewed to better understand the
  level of speeding on the street.
  5. Collision History: The collision data over the past three years
  will be studied to gain a better understanding of the street’s
  safety record and determine if implementing traffic calming
  measures would enhance safety.

Typical Recommendations in Level 2
Include:
 1. Posting of Static Signage:

  This measure aims to increase awareness of the existing or incoming road
  conditions and traffic regulations. This type of signage may include:

  A. New or Larger Speed Limit Signs:

  Installing new or larger speed limit signs enhances visibility
  and compliance with the posted speed limit, as determined
  by engineering judgment. See Figure 4 for an example of a
  New or Larger Speed Limit sign.

  i. Pros
  1. High visibility.
  2. Easy to interpret.
  3. Legal compliance.
  ii. Cons
  1. Increased enforcement may be needed to be
  effective.
  2. Added initial cost and maintenance of additional
  signs.
  iii. Cost: Low

  14 | P a g e
DRAFT TRAFFIC CALMING GUIDELINES  CITY OF ALHAMBRA
   Figure 4: Example of a new speed limit sign.

  15 | P a g e
DRAFT TRAFFIC CALMING GUIDELINES  CITY OF ALHAMBRA
   B. Larger Stop Signs With Red Reflective Strips:

  Larger sizes can enhance visibility. All-way stop plaques at all-
  way stops and red retroreflective strips on the signposts. See
  Figure 5 for an example of a Larger Stop Sign with Red
  Reflective Strips.

  i. Pros
  1. Low cost.
  2. It can usually be added to an existing signpost.
  ii. Cons
  1. Additional cost and maintenance.
  iii. Cost: Low

  16 | P a g e
DRAFT TRAFFIC CALMING GUIDELINES  CITY OF ALHAMBRA
   Figure 5: Example of a larger stop sign

  17 | P a g e
DRAFT TRAFFIC CALMING GUIDELINES  CITY OF ALHAMBRA
   C. Advanced Warning Signage:

  Advanced Warning Signs alert drivers to upcoming
  conditions that require increased caution and preparedness.
  These signs may include Signal Ahead, Stop Ahead,
  Pedestrian Crossing Ahead, Intersection Crossing Ahead,
  Curve warning signs, and other warning signs designed to
  enhance safety by providing advance notice of roadway
  conditions or traffic control changes. This could include
  adjacent pavement legends per engineering judgment. See
  Figure 6 for an example of Advanced Warning Signage.

  i. Pros
  1. Reduced risk of sudden braking.
  2. Enhanced traffic flow operations.
  3. Alerting motorists of unexpected roadway features.
  4. Safety for vulnerable road users.
  ii. Cons
  1. Additional initial cost and maintenance.
  2. Potential sign clutter on residential streets.
  iii. Cost: Low

  Figure 6: Example of advanced warning sign

  18 | P a g e
DRAFT TRAFFIC CALMING GUIDELINES  CITY OF ALHAMBRA
   D. Advisory Speed Plaque: Advisory Speed Plaques
  combined with warning signs provide critical visual
  information about upcoming roadway conditions, helping
  drivers adjust their speed accordingly. These signs may be
  combined with Curve Warning Ahead, Speed Hump Ahead,
  Hill Ahead, and Dip Ahead signs, among others. They are
  typically placed where roadway geometry or surface
  conditions require reduced speeds to enhance safety. See
  Figure 7 for an example of an Advisory Speed Plaque used for
  speed recommendations.
  i. Pros
  1. Enhanced safety.
  2. Alerts drivers to conditions that require
  caution and speed reduction.
  ii. Cons
  1. Drivers are not always compliant.
  iii. Cost: Low

  Figure 7: Example of an Advisory Speed Plaque for a Curve Warning Sign

  19 | P a g e
DRAFT TRAFFIC CALMING GUIDELINES  CITY OF ALHAMBRA
   2. Pavement Markings and Legends:

  Similar to Static Signage, Pavement Markings and/or Legends
  create awareness of existing or incoming road conditions. Examples
  of typical pavement markings include:

  A. “25 MPH”: Numerical speed markings on the pavement serve
  as a visual reminder to reinforce the posted speed limit and
  encourage compliance. These markings are typically placed
  before speed limit changes or within speed transition zones to
  enhance driver awareness. See Figure 8 for an example of
  “25 MPH” numerical speed markings on pavement used to
  reinforce the speed limit.

  i. Pros
  1. Reinforcement of speed limit.
  2. Potential for reduced collisions.
  3. Consistency with traffic regulations.
  ii. Cons
  1. Additional maintenance needs.
  2. Not suitable for all roads.
  3. Perceived visual impacts.
  iii. Cost: Low

  Figure 8: Example of 25 MPH numerical speed markings on pavement used to reinforce the
  speed limit.

  20 | P a g e
DRAFT TRAFFIC CALMING GUIDELINES  CITY OF ALHAMBRA
   B. Advance Warning Legends:

  The “Stop Ahead,” “Slow School Crossing,” “Dip Ahead,” and
  “Ped Crossing” pavement markings can be combined with
  the appropriate warning signs and serve as advance
  warnings for drivers, alerting them to upcoming stop signs
  and pedestrian crossings, respectively. See Figures 9 and 10
  for examples of these pavement markings in use.

  i. Pros
  1. Reduced intersection crashes.
  2. Cost-effective solution.
  3. Supplemental safety measures.
  4. Reduced pedestrian risk.
  ii. Cons
  1. Possible visibility issues due to the weather.
  2. Possible lack of clarity.
  iii. Cost: Low

  21 | P a g e
DRAFT TRAFFIC CALMING GUIDELINES  CITY OF ALHAMBRA
   Figure 9: Example of "STOP AHEAD" pavement markings that warn drivers of an upcoming stop
  sign.

  Figure 10: Example of pedestrian warning pavement markings (“Ped Crossing” and
  “Slow School Crossing”) to increase awareness of pedestrians.

  22 | P a g e
DRAFT TRAFFIC CALMING GUIDELINES  CITY OF ALHAMBRA
   3. Stripping of White Edge Lines/Side Stripes:

  Drivers tend to feel more comfortable driving at higher speeds
  when wider lanes have fewer obstructions. Narrowing travel lanes
  reduces a driver’s field of view and creates a psychological effect
  that encourages drivers to decrease their speed to stay within their
  lane. Edge lines and lane-narrowing techniques should be
  strategically applied to influence driver behavior without altering
  the physical infrastructure. See Figure 11 for an example of White
  Side stripes used to visually narrow lanes and reduce driving
  speeds.

  A. Pros
  i. Enhancing pedestrian and cyclist safety.
  ii. Better delineation of the parking lane when parking is
  allowed.
  iii. Low-cost safety measures.
  iv. Traffic calming.
  v. Enhanced nighttime visibility.
  B. Cons
  i. Increased maintenance of painted lines.
  ii. Limited effectiveness without additional signage.
  C. Cost: Low

  Figure 11: Example of white side stripes used to visually narrow lanes and reduce driving speeds.

  23 | P a g e
DRAFT TRAFFIC CALMING GUIDELINES  CITY OF ALHAMBRA
   4. Turning Movement Restrictions:

  Regulatory signs indicating restrictions, such as “No Right Turn,” “No
  Left Turn,” and “No U-Turn,” may help control traffic flow and
  improve intersection safety or serve as a tool to decrease cut-
  through traffic on a residential street during certain hours. These
  restrictions may apply at all times or only during certain hours. See
  Figure 12 for an example of turning movement restriction signage,
  such as “No Right Turn,” “No Left Turn,” and “No U-Turn.”

  A. Pros
  i. Significant exclusion of undesired movements
  may have a positive impact on residential
  streets.
  ii. In case of turn prohibitions, safety may be enhanced on
  residential streets where considerable unwanted traffic
  has been parked.
  B. Cons
  i. Prohibition is subject to deliberate violation,
  particularly at low-volume local intersections within the
  neighborhood where Police presence is infrequent.
  ii. Safety may decrease at other locations if drivers are
  forced to make movements to compensate for
  restricted movements.
  iii. This will impact residents who live on the street.
  Resident notification and/or petition should be
  collected if the sign is non-safety related.
  C. Cost: Low

  24 | P a g e
DRAFT TRAFFIC CALMING GUIDELINES  CITY OF ALHAMBRA
   Figure 12: Example of turning movement
  restriction signage, such as “No U-Turn,” “No
  Right Turn,” and “No Left Turn.”

  25 | P a g e
DRAFT TRAFFIC CALMING GUIDELINES  CITY OF ALHAMBRA
   5. School Area Enhancements:

  These improvements may include a combination of signage and
  pavement markings. These enhancements are aimed at reminding
  drivers of the presence of schools and pedestrians in the vicinity.
  Signage and markings are specific to school zones, including
  School signs and associated pavement markings, which focus on
  Traffic Control for School Areas. School signs should be installed in
  a neon fluorescent green. See Figure 13 for an example of School
  Area Enhancements, including Signage and Pavement Markings
  for School Zones.

  A. Pros
  i. Increased driver awareness.
  ii. Enhanced pedestrian safety.
  iii. Regulatory compliance.
  B. Cons
  i. Effectiveness depends on enforcement.
  ii. Maintenance requirements.
  C. Cost: Low

  26 | P a g e
DRAFT TRAFFIC CALMING GUIDELINES  CITY OF ALHAMBRA
   Figure 13: Example of school area enhancements,
  including signage and pavement markings for
  school zones.

  27 | P a g e
DRAFT TRAFFIC CALMING GUIDELINES  CITY OF ALHAMBRA
   6. Crossing Guard Program:

  A crossing guard program involves deploying trained personnel to
  assist pedestrians, particularly schoolchildren, safely crossing streets
  at designated crosswalks. These guards typically operate during
  school peak hours, such as school drop-off and pick-up times,
  ensuring pedestrians can cross safely, even in busy or high-traffic

   5. Traffic Circle

   6. Speed Humps, Speed Cushions, and Speed Tables:

The City is committed to policies and actions that can foster and promote
traffic calming measures whenever necessary to maximize and enhance the
safety of pedestrians, bicyclists and the general motorists traveling on city
residential streets. Important factors in enhancing traffic safety are measures
that can be implemented to slow the speed of vehicles to an appropriate
speed. One possible means to accomplish these goals is a "roadway vertical
deflection device," which is commonly known as a Speed Hump or a Speed
Cushion.

Speed Humps, Speed Cushions, and Speed Tables and similar pavement
undulations such as rumble strips are not classified as traffic control devices
under the CA MUTCD, the official standard for traffic control installations
on public streets. Instead, these devices are considered geometric
roadway design features. As such, their installation must be guided by
sound engineering judgment and supported by a thorough assessment of
need, ensuring that their implementation does not result in property
damage, personal injury, or potential liability. Once these devices are
installed, all signs and pavement markings needed to warn motorists of an
upcoming roadway feature shall be in accordance with CA MUTCD
guidelines.

These Speed Hump Guidelines are primarily intended for use in
residential neighborhoods, where traffic calming measures are most
commonly needed. While speed humps, speed tables, and speed
cushions are generally not installed in industrial or commercially zoned
areas, exceptions may be considered. If a thorough and procedural
engineering analysis determines that speed humps, speed tables, and
speed cushions are warranted in these areas due to documented safety
concerns, the guidelines may still be applied. In all cases, installation must
be supported by a petition and evaluated based on the merits of the
location, including traffic volume, speed data, and overall safety
conditions.

Speed Humps are wave-shaped paved humps in the street. The height

  44 | P a g e
DRAFT TRAFFIC CALMING GUIDELINES  CITY OF ALHAMBRA
 of the speed hump determines how fast it may be navigated without
causing discomfort to the driver or damage to the vehicle. Discomfort
increases as speed over the hump increases. Typically speed humps are
placed in a series rather than singularly. See Figure 24 for Speed Hump
usage.

Speed Cushions are a type of speed hump that include wheel cutouts to
allow large vehicles such as fire trucks to pass unaffected while reducing
passenger car speeds. Police Department, Paramedics, and other small
departmental emergency vehicles will still be impacted by the presence
of Speed Cushions. Same as Speed Humps, Speed Cushions extend
across the entire width of the street with a longitudinal gap provided to
allow wide- wheelbase vehicles to avoid going over the hump. See
Figure 25 for an example of Speed Cushion usage.

Speed Tables are similar to speed humps but are much wider, typically
ranging between 20 and 25 feet in width, compared to the 12-foot-wide
speed humps commonly used on residential streets. They have a flat top
that raises the entire wheelbase of a vehicle to reduce its traffic speed,
allowing vehicles to traverse them more smoothly while reducing speeds.
Some agencies have implemented Speed Tables on collector streets with
posted speed limits of 30 – 35 mph, as they provide a more gradual speed
reduction than traditional speed humps. Additionally, they can be
designed as raised midblock crossings, often in conjunction with curb
extensions, to enhance pedestrian safety and visibility while maintaining
reasonable traffic flow. See Figures 26 and 27 for an example of a Speed
Table in use.

  A. Pros
  i. Reduced vehicle speeds in the vicinity of the hump.
  ii. Self-enforcing.
  B. Cons
  i. They create some noise, especially in adjacent homes.
  ii. Drivers may skirt around to avoid impact.
  iii. May impact drainage.

 Definitions
The following are definitions or explanations of terminology used in this
report.

  1. Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) is federal legislation that
  mandates the provision of access while restricting impediments for
  people with disabilities and establishes many criteria and standards
  for such access. These are also contained in State Title 24 for
  California Building Standards and Codes.

  2. Average Daily Traffic (ADT) is the total number of vehicles that
  travel (both directions combined) along a roadway in a typical 24-
  hour period, usually counted on a midweek day.

  3. Collector Street is a roadway that moves traffic from local streets
  to arterial roadways, and vice versa. Speed limits could range
  from 25 to 35 MPH. Collector streets could carry one to two lanes
  in each direction.

  4. National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System (NPDES) is a
  program that addresses water pollution by regulating point sources
  that discharge pollutants to waters of the United States. Created in
  1972 by the Clean Water Act, the NPDES permit program is
  authorized to state governments by the Environmental Protection
  Agency (EPA).

  5. Gutter Running describes the situation where motorists purposely
  drive close to the gutter, so the right-side wheels (nearest the curb)
  miss the end of the speed hump. This is often done due to the
  perception of some motorists that, since fewer wheels cross over
  the speed hump, they do not need to slow for the speed hump.

  6. Local Street is a roadway that serves individual residential and
  commercial blocks with direct access to abutting properties.

  50 | P a g e
DRAFT TRAFFIC GUIDELINES  CITY OF ALHAMBRA
   Speed limits on all local residential streets are 25 MPH.

  7. Prima Facie Speed Limits are speed limits that are automatically
  established by law based on roadway conditions and therefore do
  not require signs for enforcement. Examples include 25 miles-per-
  hour limits in school zones when children are present or on local
  streets in residential neighborhoods, and 15 miles-per-hour limits
  in alleys or at railroad crossings with limited visibility. These
  speeds are defined in the California Vehicle Code as well as the
  California Manual on Uniform Traffic Control Devices.

  8. Critical Speed (85th Percentile) is a speed measurement where 85
  percent of the individually recorded vehicle speeds on the street are
  at or below this measurement, and 15 percent of the recorded speeds
  are above this measurement.

  9. Speed hump is a moderately elevated segment of roadway
  pavement intended to reduce the speed of vehicles crossing over it.
  Sloping upward, a speed hump is usually elevated about 3 or 4 inches
  before it slopes downward to the original street level. The overall
  crossing length of a speed hump is about 12 feet wide. (Shorter,
  steeper speed bumps are used in private parking lots but are too
  extreme an obstacle for use on a public street).

  10.  Speed Cushions are speed humps that include wheel cutouts to
  allow large vehicles to pass unaffected, while reducing passenger car
  speeds. They can be offset to allow unimpeded passage by fire trucks
  and are typically used on key emergency response routes.

  11. Speed Tables are similar to speed humps but are much wider and
  typically range between 20-30 feet wide as compared to 12 feet wide
  for speed humps used on residential streets. Some agencies have
  used speed tables on collector streets with speeds of 30-35 mph.

  1. A n applicant must complete and submit a “Citizen Request

  2. Once measures have been recommended and installed from Level 1
  and Level 2, and has been determined that prior measures were not
  effective in reducing vehicular speed on the roadway, Level 3
  measures such as speed humps will be considered. The resident is
  asked to resubmit the request, stating that Level 1 and 2 measures
  were not effective, and would like the City to consider Level 3 measures

  determine if the street in question meets the basic “non data” criteria
  for speed hump/cushion applications. These criteria can be found

  process of investigating the request which will include collecting traffic
  and speeding data to assess the Eligibility Criteria listed below.

  5. If, at the end of the City Staff’s investigation, the street does not meet
  the Eligibility Criteria, the City Staff will inform the requester (contact
  person) and report the findings to the Transportation Commission,
  where members of the public may also attend to provide their input.

  Humps, Speed Tables, and Speed Cushions, City Staff will supply the

 Eligibility Criteria
Each request will be reviewed following the eligibility criteria on a case-by-
case basis. The Department will determine the streets that are eligible for
speed humps/cushions based on site and roadway conditions, traffic
conditions, and proper engineering principles, including, but not limited to,
the following:

  1. The street must be functionally classified as a residential, collector, or
  local street with a maximum street width of 40’ curb-to-curb. The
  street cannot be designated as an arterial or higher classification.

  2. The street should be primarily residential in land use, but streets in
  commercially or industrially zoned areas can be eligible for speed
  humps, consistent with engineering analysis and safety concerns.

  3. The street should not be a truck route, transit (bus) route, or a
  primary emergency service route.

  4. The street should not have more than one traffic lane in each direction.

  5. The street should have a minimum length of at least 700 feet with no
  traffic signals or stop signs existing less than 700 feet apart along the
  street segment(s). This typically will include a long block, or two to
  three short blocks with no stop signs or traffic signals at each end.

  6. Speed humps are generally not recommended for cul-de-sacs as there
  is no through traffic and traffic volumes are primarily generated by
  residents of the cul-de-sac. Cul-de-sacs meeting the speeding,
  length, and volume requirements may be considered for the
  application of speed humps based on engineering judgment.

  7. The street must have a posted or prima facie speed limit not
  exceeding 25 miles per hour.

   8. The street must have a critical or 85% speed of 34 mph or more.

  9. The street must have a minimum ADT volume of 1,000 average daily
  vehicle trips and a maximum ADT volume of 4,000 vehicles per day.

  10.  The street must have adequate drainage and ADA access at
  street entrances and intersections.

  11.  The street must have roadway pavement, curbs, gutters,
  adjoining parkways, and sidewalks in good condition.

  12.  The street cannot have any alignment, grade, or sight-distance
  limitations that would be affected or created by speed humps.
  Speed hump, Speed Tables, Speed Cushion are not
  recommended on streets having a grade of more than 5%.

  13.  Speed hump, Speed Tables, Speed Cushion should not be

Standard
  1. Spacing. Speed humps should not be spaced closer than 200 feet
  when two humps are installed on a single block and should not be
  spaced closer than 350 feet when three humps are installed on a
  single block. If needed, the City will adjust the spacing in between
  the speed humps accordingly for optimal operations. A speed
  hump generally should not be placed within 75 to 100 feet of any
  intersection. A speed hump shall never be installed within any
  intersection.

  2. Conflicts. A speed hump should not be installed if it conflicts
  or interferes with:

  a. Drainage features include gutters, channels, drains, catch
  basins, and manholes.
  b. Compliance with NPDES regulations for stormwater run-off.
  c. Fire hydrants, water valves, water meters, utility manholes, or
  other utility facilities.
  d. Traffic control devices, including in-pavement signal detector
  devices.
  e. Driveways, crosswalks, ramps, and/or other ADA
  facilities/regulations.
  f. Bicycle lanes.
  g. Horizontal or vertical curves in the street alignment or street profile.

  3. Roadway Edge. A speed hump should not extend across the full
  width of the roadway (curb-to-curb) to permit unobstructed water
  flow along the curb and gutter. The end of the speed hump should
  be separated from the curb at a distance sufficient to permit street-
  sweeping machinery to pass along the curb and gutter without
  affecting the operation of the street-sweeper and/or without
  causing swept debris to be left in the roadway. Each end of the
  speed hump must taper at a sufficiently low angle so that it will not

  4. Installation Angle. A speed hump must be installed exactly at a
  right angle to the vehicular path of travel.

  5. Pavement Markings. Speed humps will be painted with
  distinctive painted markings so as to be readily visible to
  approaching vehicles.

  6. Signs. Speed hump signs whose design and locations are in
  compliance with the CAMUTCD shall be installed to provide
  appropriate forewarning of the presence and location of speed
  humps to approaching vehicles. Additional sign plates should
  be installed to indicate the recommended crossing speed to
  educate motorists when the speed humps are initially installed.

  7. On-Street Parking. Care should be taken to ensure vehicles
  parked on streets do not diminish the effectiveness of signs and/or
  pavement markings. The potential for "gutter running" should be
  considered in locating a speed hump if parking is prohibited along
  the curb, either permanently or for limited times (e.g., street-
  sweeping). On the other hand, curbside parking may be restricted
  or prohibited in the vicinity of a speed hump if parked vehicles are
  at an increased risk of being damaged by vehicles crossing the
  speed hump.

  8. Street Lighting. Where sight distance is less than desirable and/or
  to improve nighttime visibility, speed hump locations should be
  selected with existing or planned street lighting.

  9. Pedestrian Crossings. The positioning of a speed hump must
  fully comply with ADA regulations for pedestrian walkways and
  crosswalks. If mid-block pedestrian crossings are planned, it may be
  appropriate to coordinate their design with speed humps since
  vehicle speeds will generally be slower at speed hump crossings.

  speed hump profile must be maintained to ensure that the desired

  vehicle damage or ineffective speed control. Road surfaces must be

  12 months prior to any scheduled roadway repairs, resurfacing or
  reconstruction, or utility excavations within the roadway. If such work
  is planned, speed hump installation should be incorporated into the
  scheduled repairs or reconstruction projects.

  12. Maintenance. Care should be taken in the initial installation and

  Regularly scheduled inspections and maintenance should be

  speed hump to continue to perform it intended purpose. Speed
  hump markings need to be regularly monitored and refreshed to
  maintain high visibility to motorists.

 Speed Hump/Cushion Removal Criteria
Following an adequate review and analysis period, a speed
hump/cushion can be removed if a traffic circulation and traffic safety
study justify the removal of the speed hump. Any requested or proposed
removal pursuant to these guidelines shall require the approval of the City
Council. The temporary removal of a speed hump to permit the
reconstruction of the speed hump or the reconstruction or resurfacing of
the street, provided that the speed hump will be restored thereafter, is
exempt from requiring City Council approval. Permanent removal of
Speed Humps requested by area residents shall follow these steps:

  1. Petition – Signed by the property owners, renters, or residents of at
  least 67% of the homes on the street and verified by an independent
  survey conducted by City staff, no less than 2 years after the
  installation date.

  2. Notification of Residents – Following receipt of a petition to
  remove a speed hump, the City shall notify each property owners,
  renters, or residents of the subject street at least two weeks prior to
  consideration of the item by the Transportation Commission.

  3. Staff Review – City staff shall conduct appropriate studies of traffic
  volume and speed, area conditions, collision history, diversion of
  traffic to/from adjacent streets, and overall effectiveness of the
  speed hump(s). Conduct an independent survey to verify 67%
  support for the removal of the speed humps.

  4. Transportation Commission Review – The Transportation
  Commission will review and consider the staff report, receive citizen
  input, and make recommendations as to whether the speed humps
  shall be removed.

  5. City Council – The City Council shall consider the Transportation
  Commission’s recommendation, receive citizen input, and make the

   final determination as to whether the speed humps shall be removed
  subject to availability of funds.

  6. Reinstallation – If speed humps are removed at the request of the
  property owners, renters, or residents and there is a subsequent
  request for reinstallation, such requests will only be considered
  after five years from the date of the removal.

Installation Guidelines
 1. Hump Dimensions – Full height shall generally extend to 2 feet from
  the gutter and taper to join existing pavement at the edge of the
  gutter.

 2. Spacing – 300 feet to 500 feet. 25 feet to fire hydrants, driveways, or
  manholes. Generally, a minimum of 75 to 100 feet from an
  intersection.

 3. Warning  Signs – “HUMPS AHEAD” signs shall be placed
  approximately 250 feet prior to the first hump. “HUMP” signs shall
  be placed approximately 50 feet prior to each hump.

 4. Markings – “HUMP” pavement markings shall be placed
  approximately 50 feet prior to each hump. Reflective solid white
  striping shall be placed on the hump in such a manner as to bring
  attention to the change in roadway conditions.

 Requests for All-Way Stop or Signal Modifications

STOP SIGNS: Stop signs and traffic signals are classified as traffic control
devices rather than traffic calming measures and are intended to regulate
traffic flow and assign the right-of-way. Their installation is determined by
warrants specified in the CA MUTCD and the CVC, which consider factors
such as traffic volume, pedestrian crossings, available gaps in traffic,
collision history, and the results of a comprehensive engineering study.
When concerns about speeding are received and as a result a request
for All-Way Stop Control (AWSC), a Level 1 review must be conducted,
which includes notifying the Police Department Traffic Division for
enforcement of speeds. CA MUTCD Section 2B.04 specifies that stop signs
should not be used as speed control measures, as their primary purpose
is to assign right-of-way, not to reduce speed. If speeding is a concern,
other traffic calming measures from Levels 2 and 3 should be considered.
A three-year review of collision records may be performed to assess safety
issues of an intersection before a comprehensive warrant study is
completed for an intersection.

TRAFFIC SIGNALS: Traffic signals are normally not applicable for
installation on residential street intersections. When traffic volumes and
delays are justified, they may be placed at the intersection of some
residential streets with major arterial streets.

The installation of new traffic signals involves significant costs and requires a
thorough engineering study by Section 4C of the CA MUTCD. Funding must
be identified before initiating the investigation, with many cities relying on
grant funding to cover the costs of a new traffic signal or modifications of an
existing signal. A proper line of sight is essential for stop signs and traffic
signals to function effectively. These devices must be clearly visible to drivers
and pedestrians and free from obstructions like trees, signage, or buildings.
Proper signage must be placed to ensure visibility from all directions,
including intersection approaches, and signals should be positioned at an
appropriate height and angle for easy visibility. Additionally, clear zones must
be maintained around traffic control devices to avoid visual barriers. By
